objectives: Distinguish subtractive, FM, additive, wavetable, granular synthesis.
Outline the analog-style synthesizer signal chain.

slides.title: Subtractive synthesis: the analog model
slides.body:
**Subtractive synthesis**: start with a harmonically-rich waveform; SUBTRACT (filter) frequencies to shape the tone.

**Classic analog signal chain** (Moog, ARP, Roland Jupiter):
```
Oscillator(s) → Mixer → Filter (VCF) → Amplifier (VCA) → Output
                        ↑              ↑
                  Envelope (ADSR) → Envelope (ADSR)
                  LFO modulation
```

**Oscillator (VCO — Voltage Controlled Oscillator)**:
- **Sine**: pure tone, single frequency. Used for sub-bass.
- **Triangle**: smoother than square; some harmonics.
- **Sawtooth**: all harmonics. Bright, buzzy.
- **Square / pulse**: odd harmonics. Hollow.
- **PWM (Pulse Width Modulation)**: varying pulse width creates time-varying timbre.

Digital VAs (Virtual Analog) use band-limited oscillators (PolyBLEP, MinBLEP) to avoid aliasing.

**Filter (VCF — Voltage Controlled Filter)**: heart of the sound.
- **Low-pass (most common)**: removes highs above cutoff.
- **High-pass**: removes lows.
- **Band-pass**: passes a range.
- **Notch**: removes a range.
- **Resonance**: feedback at cutoff frequency; can self-oscillate.

**Envelope (ADSR — Attack, Decay, Sustain, Release)**:
- **Attack**: rise time to peak.
- **Decay**: fall to sustain level.
- **Sustain**: held level while key down.
- **Release**: fall to zero after key release.

**LFO (Low Frequency Oscillator)**: sub-audio modulator. Wobbles parameters (filter cutoff for wah, pitch for vibrato, amplitude for tremolo).

**Amplifier (VCA — Voltage Controlled Amplifier)**: gates the sound based on envelope. Controls dynamics.

**Modulation matrix**: route LFOs + envelopes to ANY parameter. The flexibility that makes analog-style synths expressive. Modern softsynths (Massive X, Serum, Phase Plant) have huge modulation matrices.

slides.title: FM + additive + wavetable + granular
slides.body:
**FM (Frequency Modulation) synthesis** (Chowning 1973, Yamaha DX7 1983): one oscillator's frequency modulates another's. Generates rich, complex spectra from simple primitives. Bell tones, metallic timbres, electric pianos. DX7's iconic electric piano sound was FM.

Math: $y(t) = \sin(2\pi f_c t + I \sin(2\pi f_m t))$. Modulating wave at $f_m$ shifts carrier's instantaneous frequency. Index $I$ controls modulation depth. Frequencies + modulation depth determine harmonic content.

**Additive synthesis**: build complex sound by ADDING many sine waves with different frequencies + amplitudes + envelopes. Each partial separately controlled. Powerful but expensive (CPU + parameter count).

Notable additive synths: Hammond organ (sliders for harmonic levels), Kawai K5, modern: Loom, Razor, Image-Line Harmor.

**Wavetable synthesis**: oscillator's waveshape is a TABLE of samples that can be morphed across position. Each table position is a single-cycle waveform. Sweep through table for evolving tone. Used in Serum, Vital, Massive X, Pigments. The defining synthesis of modern electronic + EDM.

**Sample-based + ROMpler**: triggered samples instead of synthesized oscillators. Kontakt, Omnisphere, Native Instruments libraries. Best of both: realistic acoustic emulations + synthesis flexibility.

**Granular synthesis**: chop audio into tiny grains (~10-100 ms); rearrange / loop / pitch-shift them. Creates atmospheric textures from any source material. Used in cinematic + ambient music. Examples: Granulator (Ableton), Output Portal, Output Movement.

**Physical modeling**: simulate physics of acoustic instruments (struck strings, plucked, bowed, blown). Used in pianos, percussion, wind. Examples: Pianoteq, Roland VP-9000, Logic Sculpture.

**Modular synthesis**: connect components freely (oscillators, filters, envelopes, modulators) via patch cables. Eurorack (1990s+) revived modular. Software equivalents: VCV Rack, Bitwig Modules.

**Modern hybrid synths** (Serum, Phase Plant, Pigments, Massive X): combine multiple synthesis types: wavetable + FM + analog + sample + granular. Unprecedented sonic flexibility.

slides.title: Polyphony + voice management
slides.body:
**Polyphony**: number of simultaneous notes a synth can play.

- **Monophonic**: one note at a time. Classic Minimoog, Yamaha CS-10. Many bass + lead synths.
- **Polyphonic**: multiple notes. From 4-voice (Oberheim 4-Voice) to ~64+ voices in modern softsynths.
- **Unison**: same note across multiple voices, detuned slightly. Thick, wide sound. Common for leads + supersaws.

**Voice stealing**: when polyphony limit reached + new note triggered. Drop oldest, lowest-velocity, or oldest-with-release. Algorithm choices affect feel.

**Voice management challenges**:
- **CPU**: each voice = oscillators + filters + envelopes computed in parallel. 32 voices × 4 oscillators × 1024 samples per buffer = lots of compute.
- **Latency**: must initiate voice in same buffer as MIDI note. Plugins set audio callback latencies typically ≤6 ms.
- **Glide / portamento**: smooth pitch transitions in monophonic mode.
- **Legato vs retrigger**: when sliding to a new note, retrigger envelope or continue?

**Synthesis CPU bottleneck**: modern softsynths can use 5-30% CPU per instance with all features (oversampling, multiple oscillators, filter modeling). Stack 10+ instances + a track gets heavy. Bouncing to audio = standard performance hack.

**Latency-vs-quality plugin design**:
- Lookahead processing (transient detection, linear-phase EQ) increases latency.
- Compensated by DAW automatically.
- Live performance: zero-latency settings prioritized.

**Plugin formats**: VST3, AU (Apple), AAX (Pro Tools), CLAP (modern open). Cross-platform plugins built once + targeted at multiple formats. CLAP is gaining ground as open standard for innovative plugin features (per-note modulation, polyphonic modulation routing).

**MPE (MIDI Polyphonic Expression)**: each NOTE has independent per-channel pitch bend + modulation. Enables expressive per-finger control (ROLI Seaboard, Linnstrument, Lightpad). Modern softsynths increasingly support MPE.

question.question: Compute FM synthesis spectrum
question.goal: FM synth: carrier $f_c = 200$ Hz, modulator $f_m = 100$ Hz, modulation index $I = 2$. Bessel-function analysis gives sidebands at $f_c \pm n f_m$ for $n = 0, 1, 2, ...$

steps.reveal: Positive sidebands: 300, 400, 500, ... Hz. 'Negative' sidebands wrap: 100, 0 (DC), -100→100 Hz (sign flip is phase). Full spectrum at 0, 100, 200, 300, 400, ... Hz.

options: n=1 sidebands at $f_c \pm f_m$ = 100 + 300 Hz. Largest Bessel amplitude at this modulation index.

steps.reveal: n=1 sidebands (100 + 300 Hz). At modulation index $I$, peak Bessel coefficient shifts: $I=0$ → only carrier; $I=1$ → spread to J_0/J_1; higher I → wider spectrum.

steps.prompt: If $f_c$ / $f_m$ ratio is INTEGER (200/100 = 2 here), spectrum is HARMONIC. If non-integer, INHARMONIC (bell-like). FM's signature trick.

options: Integer ratios → harmonic series → 'pitched' instrument timbres (electric piano, bass). Non-integer → inharmonic spectra → bells, gongs, metallic percussion. Classic FM trick for synthetic bells.

steps.reveal: Integer $f_c/f_m$ → pitched tones. Irrational ratios → bells. DX7 patches exploit this — change ratios for different instrument families. Yamaha's 'algorithm' was the connectivity pattern (which operator modulated which).

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{FM: spectrum at } f_c \pm n f_m \text{, amplitudes from Bessel } J_n(I)}$$ FM's beauty: rich, complex spectra from 2 oscillators + an index. The DX7's 32 voices × 6 operators × 32 algorithms produced an enormous variety of sounds from minimal hardware. Yamaha shipped 200K+ DX7s in the 1980s. FM remains a staple in modern softsynths (FM8, Phase Plant, Serum's FM mode).

question.question: A user complains that their softsynth 'cuts out' notes when playing chords. Likely cause?
options: Polyphony limit reached → voice stealing. Increase polyphony cap in synth settings. Trade-off: more voices = more CPU. Bouncing to audio reduces real-time CPU + frees up resources.
question.explanation: Synth voice stealing: when polyphony limit (typically 8-64 voices) reached, new notes steal oldest/quietest. Symptoms: chords cut, sustained notes drop, expressive parts lose detail. Fix: raise voice limit. Cost: CPU. Hot-track plugins can use 30%+ CPU per instance with heavy patches. Bouncing problematic tracks to audio frees CPU. Many synths default to 16-32 voices; increase for piano/chord-heavy use.

slides.workedSolution: Voice stealing: when voice limit reached, oldest/quietest voice replaced by new note. Algorithms vary; some prioritize sustain-on, others time-since-on. Symptoms: cut chords, dropped sustained notes. Fixes: increase poly limit (more CPU), bounce to audio, use different synth, simplify patch (fewer oscillators per voice).

question.prompt: A producer wants a 'massive lead' for a track. Walk through synthesis choices: oscillator type, unison voices, filter, modulation.
Explain in two or three sentences why wavetable synthesis became the dominant synthesis paradigm in modern electronic music production.
question.rubric: Mentions that wavetable enables vast timbre variation by morphing through tables; combines harmonic richness of analog with computational efficiency + UI tractability; allows artists to create complex evolving tones with simpler modulation routes. Serum + Vital + Massive X have made wavetable the default for many genres.
